title: Succession Is Three Handovers, Not One
summary: Succession moves three different things from one generation to the next: ownership, control and the knowledge to run what is owned. Most plans handle only ownership. This lesson separates the three and shows where a family constitution fits.
body:
Succession is not one event at death. It is three separate handovers, ownership, control and knowledge, and a plan that only moves ownership hands the next generation an asset it cannot run.

Recall

Q. Why might a person with property in two countries hold more than one will?

A. So that each will deals with the assets in one jurisdiction and can be proved there under local rules, which can make probate faster. The wills must be drafted together so that one does not accidentally revoke the other.

Q. What is an estate freeze, in concept?

A. A reorganisation that fixes the value of the current owner's interest at today's figure, so that future growth accrues to new shares held by the next generation or a trust. The mechanics and tax treatment depend on local law.

Q. What is a liquidity tier in wealth architecture?

A. A layer of assets grouped by how fast it can become cash without loss: cash, near-cash, and long-term illiquid holdings such as land and buildings.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a developer builds assets that outlive projects. A completed building, a land bank, a company with a track record and lender relationships: these are worth most when someone competent keeps running them. The phrase you will hear most often in family enterprises is that wealth rarely survives three generations. Treat that as a common observation rather than a measured statistic, because the precise figures quoted for it are hard to source. The pattern behind it is real: families transfer the shares, then discover nobody can run what the shares own, or that two heirs who each own half cannot agree on anything.

Kema joins me this week because succession is as much about people as about documents. The documents are the easy part.

The three handovers

Plain English first. Imagine a hypothetical founder who owns a development company. When she steps back, three things must move.

Ownership is who holds the shares, the units in a trust, or the title to land. It decides who receives value. It is moved by wills, trusts, share transfers and estate freezes, which you studied in the last three weeks.

Control is who decides. In a company that means who sits on the board, who holds the voting shares, and who signs. Control and ownership can be split on purpose: a founder can give away economic value while keeping voting control, or the reverse.

Knowledge is the ability to run the business: the lender relationships, the judgement about when to buy land, the contractors who answer the phone. Knowledge cannot be transferred by document. It is transferred by years of supervised work.

The professional framing is that succession means the planned transfer of ownership, control and leadership of family wealth or a family enterprise from one generation to the next. A plan is incomplete until it names, for each of the three, who receives it, when, and on what conditions.

Applied example, with hypothetical numbers. A founder holds a company worth 12,000,000 dollars, with three adult children. Her will leaves the shares equally. That moves ownership. It says nothing about control, so each child holds one third of the votes, and nothing about knowledge, because none of them has worked in the business. On her death the company has three equal owners, no designated leader and a lender who wants to know who signs. That is not a succession plan. It is a division of shares.

Say that out loud now.

Where the family constitution fits

A family constitution is a written statement, agreed by family members, of the family's values, how family wealth and any family business will be governed, and how decisions affecting the family's shared assets will be made. Some families call it a family charter or family protocol.

It usually covers who may work in the family business and on what terms, how family members are paid compared with outsiders, how the family council meets, how disputes are handled, and how shares may be sold or passed on. In most places it is largely a moral and governance document rather than a binding contract. Its teeth come from the legal documents that implement it: the shareholders' agreement, the company's articles, and any trust deed. Day 4 covers that distinction.

Applied example. A hypothetical family agrees in its constitution that a child may join the company only after four years of outside employment and must report to a non-family manager for the first two years. The shareholders' agreement then gives the board, not the parents, the decision to hire family members. The constitution states the principle. The agreement enforces it.

Fairness versus equality

The hardest word in succession is fair. Equality means everyone receives the same. Fairness means everyone receives what the family agrees they should receive, which may differ by contribution, need or role. A child who has spent fifteen years building the business may reasonably expect more control than a sibling who has not. A child with a disability may need more security. Equal shares can be deeply unfair, and unequal shares can be fair, but only if the reasoning is explained and accepted while the founder is alive to explain it.

The common professional answer is to separate the three handovers again. The active heir receives control of the operating business. Inactive heirs receive equal or near-equal economic value through other assets, insurance proceeds or a fixed income stream. Day 5 works through the numbers.

How the best do it

Long-lived family enterprises that advisers often study tend to share a few practices, which I describe without naming any family. They hold regular family assemblies separate from board meetings, so family matters do not leak into business decisions. They set entry rules for family employment and apply them. They appoint independent directors who can say no to the family. And they review the constitution on a schedule, because the family changes as children marry and grandchildren arrive. A small developer can copy all four at almost no cost: one written page of entry rules, one independent adviser on the board, and one family meeting a year with minutes.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: each handover can trigger tax at transfer, so the timing of ownership moves matters; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: an heir who takes control may also take on guarantees and director duties, so they need to know what they are signing. Banking: lenders lend to people they trust, so introduce the successor to the bank years before they need it. Governance: the constitution and the shareholders' agreement must say the same thing. Estate: the will moves ownership, but control and knowledge need their own plan. Exit: decide in advance whether a family member may sell to outsiders, and at what price formula.

Professional sign-off required: estate lawyer, on the will, trust and shareholders' agreement; accountant or tax adviser, on the timing of transfers.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is moving ownership without moving control and knowledge, so a capable business passes to owners who cannot agree or cannot run it. The control is a written succession map with three columns, ownership, control and knowledge, each with a named person, a date and a condition, reviewed every year.

The beginner's mistake

Treating the will as the succession plan. The will is necessary and it handles only one of the three handovers. The beginner also waits for a crisis to talk to the family, when the person best placed to explain the reasoning is no longer able to.

Callback

In Week 69, JAX and LEX taught deadlock clauses and the four Ds, death, disability, divorce and departure, in partner agreements. A family business is a partnership whose partners did not choose each other. The same tools apply: a deadlock mechanism, a buy-sell clause and a price formula. Equal heirs without them are equal partners without a deadlock clause.

Recap

Succession moves ownership, control and knowledge, and each needs its own plan. A family constitution states the family's rules, and the shareholders' agreement and trust deed enforce them. Fairness and equality are different, and the founder must explain the difference while alive.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: a composite case of three equal heirs and a company nobody could run.
checklist: I can name who receives ownership, control and knowledge in my plan.
I keep a written succession map with a date and condition for each handover.
My will is not my whole succession plan.
My family constitution and shareholders' agreement say the same thing.
I have introduced any successor to my lender and key contractors.
I have explained any unequal division while I can still explain it.
I review the plan every year and after any family change.
head: Field checklist
speak: Succession is three handovers, not one. Ownership is who holds the shares and receives the value; wills, trusts and share transfers move it. Control is who decides: who sits on the board, holds the votes and signs. Knowledge is the ability to run the business, and it moves only through years of supervised work. Most plans handle only ownership. A founder who leaves her company equally to three children who have never worked in it has divided the shares, not planned a succession. A family constitution states the family's rules on employment, pay, decisions and sales of shares, and the shareholders' agreement and trust deed give those rules legal force. Fairness and equality differ: the active heir may take control while the others take equal value in other assets. Keep a written map with a person, a date and a condition for each of the three handovers, and review it every year.
terms: Succession — the planned transfer of ownership, control and leadership of family wealth or a family business to the next generation.
Family constitution — a written agreement among family members on values, governance and decision rules for shared family assets, given legal force by other documents.
Fairness versus equality — equality gives everyone the same; fairness gives each person what the family agrees is right given contribution, need and role.

hostile.q: If you were hit by a bus tomorrow, who signs the next draw on this loan, and why should I trust them?
hostile.a: My succession map names an interim signatory with board authority under a standing resolution, and a successor who has attended our lender meetings for the past period. I will send you the resolution and an introduction this week, so you are not meeting that person for the first time in a crisis.

title: Three Equal Heirs and a Company Nobody Could Run
summary: A composite case: a founder left her development company in equal thirds to three children, with no shareholders' agreement, no named successor and no deadlock mechanism. Within a few years the company was sold below value to break a deadlock. Seven forensic steps show where it could have been stopped.
body:
This is a composite example. A founder divided her company equally among three children and planned nothing else, and within a few years the family sold a healthy business at a discount simply to stop arguing.

Recall

Q. In a cross-border estate, what does probate do?

A. It is the court process that confirms a will is valid and authorises the executor to deal with the assets. Each jurisdiction where assets sit may require its own grant or recognition of a foreign one.

Q. What is attribution, in the context of transferring assets to family members?

A. A family of rules, in some tax systems, that can treat income or gains on property given to a spouse or minor as still belonging to the person who gave it. Whether and how it applies depends on local law; verify against the primary source.

Q. What is a currency reserve in personal wealth architecture?

A. Cash or near-cash held in the currency of your future obligations, so a swing in exchange rates does not force you to sell long-term assets at the wrong moment.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Cole joins me because this failure is legal and governance in nature. No law was broken. Nobody stole anything. A company that was worth more running than sold was sold anyway, because the documents that would have let the family decide did not exist. This is a composite example, assembled from patterns that recur in family businesses. Every number is a hypothetical round figure.

1. Timeline

Year 0: a founder runs a small development company that owns three rental buildings and a land bank, valued at about 15,000,000 dollars net of debt. Her eldest child has worked in the company for ten years and runs construction. The second is a doctor abroad. The third is a student. The founder's will leaves her shares in equal thirds. There is no shareholders' agreement among the future owners. Year 2: the founder dies suddenly. The eldest keeps running projects, but as a one-third shareholder and director alongside the other two, who are now directors too. Year 3: the eldest wants to buy a new site using the land bank as security. The other two want dividends. The board splits two to one against the purchase. Year 4: the eldest stops taking the low salary he accepted while his mother was alive and asks for market pay. The others refuse. Year 5: the eldest resigns. With no one running the business, the lender reviews the loans and asks for a new manager. Year 6: the siblings sell the whole company to a buyer at well below the valuation, because a buyer of a company with no management and a family dispute has all the leverage.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions shaped the outcome. Leaving voting shares equally, rather than separating votes from value. Not signing a shareholders' agreement while the founder was alive and could broker one. And allowing all three heirs to become directors automatically, without asking whether a doctor abroad and a student were the right people to direct a development company.

3. Assumptions

The founder assumed love would substitute for governance: that her children would work it out. She assumed the eldest would keep working for a below-market salary out of loyalty. She assumed that equal shares were fair. Each assumption was reasonable in a family and fatal in a company.

4. Incentives

The incentives pointed in different directions, and nobody designed them to align. The eldest was paid by salary and wanted growth, because growth was his career. The inactive siblings were paid only by dividends, so every dollar reinvested in land was a dollar they did not receive. Neither side was greedy. Each acted rationally on the incentive the will had handed them. When people's interests diverge, a governance structure decides who wins. Here there was none, so the stalemate decided, and a stalemate always favours selling.

Say that out loud now.

5. Warning signs ignored

There were four. The eldest had told his mother, years earlier, that he would not work forever on a family salary. The second child had said she had no interest in the business. The company's banker had asked who would run it if the founder were unavailable and received a vague answer. And the founder's lawyer had recommended a shareholders' agreement, which was put off because the founder did not want an awkward conversation. Each sign was spoken aloud. None was written down and acted on.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was the founder's death without a signed agreement. Before it, she could have used her authority and her personality to get three children to sign a deadlock clause, a buy-sell formula and a decision on who leads. After it, any change needed the agreement of people whose interests now diverged. Some families do negotiate an agreement after the death, but it is far harder, because every term now moves money between siblings directly.

7. Root cause

The root cause was confusing equality with a plan. The founder moved ownership equally and moved neither control nor knowledge deliberately. Cole puts it in an auditor's terms: there was no document that answered the question "who decides when the owners disagree?", and every company eventually faces that question.

Cole adds a second auditor's point. Read the company's records from Year 0 and you find no minute recording who would lead after the founder, no written salary for the eldest, and no board policy on dividends versus reinvestment. Each of those is a one-page document. Their absence meant that every later disagreement was argued from memory and feeling rather than from a record, and an argument with no record has no end. The siblings were not unusually difficult people. They had simply been given nothing to point to. When you audit your own plan, ask the same question Cole asks: if I were not here, which document would each of my heirs open to settle the first disagreement, and does it exist?

What would have stopped it

A hypothetical alternative, using the same family. The founder recapitalises: voting shares go to the eldest, and non-voting shares carrying equal economic value go to all three. A shareholders' agreement sets a dividend policy, a market salary for any family member employed, and a buy-sell clause with a formula price based on an independent valuation, so the eldest can buy out a sibling who wants cash. An independent director sits on the board. Life insurance on the founder funds part of any buyout. None of this guarantees peace. It does guarantee that a disagreement has a route to a decision other than a forced sale.

Professional sign-off required: estate lawyer and corporate lawyer, on the share structure and agreement; tax adviser, on any reorganisation of share classes.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is assuming family members will agree because they love each other, and leaving the company without a mechanism for when they do not. The control is a signed shareholders' agreement, made while the founder is alive, that names who decides, how deadlock breaks and how an exit is priced.

The beginner's mistake

Leaving every heir equal votes and an automatic seat on the board. Ownership of value and the right to direct are different, and a beginner hands out both together because it feels fair.

Callback

In Week 75, the second post-mortem looked at handshake deals and governance capture among partners. This family had the same defect from the other side: not one dominant partner, but three equal ones with no rule for breaking a tie. Whether one partner captures the company or three paralyse it, the missing document is the same.

Recap

A composite founder left equal votes to three heirs with different roles and incentives, no agreement and no successor, and the deadlock ended in a discounted sale. The point of no return was her death without a signed agreement.

Rule 93: Never pass a company to more than one heir without a signed shareholders' agreement, made in your lifetime, that names who decides, how a deadlock breaks and how an exit is priced.

Next: Warrick, on The Money: what succession costs, and how to fund equalisation without selling the business.
checklist: I have a signed shareholders' agreement among my future owners, made in my lifetime.
I have decided whether votes and value pass together or separately.
Every family member employed in the business is paid a written market rate.
There is a dividend policy, so reinvestment is not a fight each year.
There is a buy-sell clause with a formula price and an independent valuer.
At least one independent director can break a family deadlock.
I write down and act on every warning sign a family member says aloud.
head: Field checklist
speak: This is a composite case. A founder left her development company in equal thirds to three children: one who had run construction for ten years, one abroad, one a student. There was no shareholders' agreement and every heir became a director. The active son wanted to buy land and earn market pay; the others wanted dividends. Each acted on the incentive the will had handed them. The board deadlocked, the son resigned, the lender asked who would manage the loans, and the family sold the company well below value. The warning signs were all spoken aloud and none was written down. The point of no return was the founder's death without a signed agreement, because after it every term moved money between siblings. The root cause was confusing equality with a plan. Rule 93: never pass a company to more than one heir without a signed agreement, made in your lifetime, that names who decides, how deadlock breaks and how an exit is priced.
terms: Deadlock — a state where owners or directors are evenly split and no decision can be made, so the company cannot act.
Buy-sell clause — a term in a shareholders' agreement that lets or requires one owner to buy another's shares on defined events, at a defined price or formula.
Non-voting shares — shares that carry a right to dividends and value but no vote, used to separate economic benefit from control.

hostile.q: Your three shareholders are related and split. If they disagree on refinancing next year, what happens to my loan?
hostile.a: The shareholders' agreement names the eldest as holder of the voting shares and gives an independent director the casting vote on any financing within an approved policy. So a family disagreement cannot freeze a refinancing. I will send you the clause and the board resolution.

rule: Rule 93: Never pass a company to more than one heir without a signed shareholders' agreement, made in your lifetime, that names who decides, how a deadlock breaks and how an exit is priced.

title: What Succession Costs, and Who Pays for Fairness
summary: Succession has a price: tax at transfer, the value lost when a business changes hands badly, and the cash needed to treat inactive heirs fairly without selling the operating company. This lesson prices those three costs and the main ways families fund them.
body:
Fairness among heirs usually needs cash that the estate does not have, because the valuable asset is a business or a building. Decide where that cash comes from while you are alive, or the business will be sold to provide it.

Recall

Q. What is incapacity planning, and why does it matter as much as a will?

A. Arranging, through powers of attorney and similar documents, who acts for you if you are alive but cannot decide. Without it, a business can freeze because nobody has authority to sign while the owner is incapacitated.

Q. In a discretionary trust, who decides which beneficiary receives income?

A. The trustee, within the powers in the trust deed and subject to the trustee's duties. No beneficiary has a fixed entitlement until the trustee exercises its discretion.

Q. What does concentration mean on a personal balance sheet?

A. Having a large share of your net worth in one asset, market or currency, so a single event can damage most of your wealth at once.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a developer's wealth is usually illiquid and concentrated: buildings, land and shares in operating companies. That is how wealth gets built. It is also why succession goes wrong. An estate that is mostly a building has very little cash, and the costs of passing it on, and the cost of treating every heir fairly, arrive in cash. This lesson puts numbers on those costs. All figures are hypothetical round numbers.

The three costs of succession

The first cost is transfer cost: tax and fees that arise when ownership moves, such as tax on gains deemed to arise at death in some systems, transfer taxes, probate fees and legal costs. The amount and even the existence of each depend entirely on the jurisdiction. Verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

The second cost is value leakage: the drop in what the business is worth when it changes hands without a ready leader. A lender may tighten terms. Key staff may leave. A buyer who knows the family must sell pays less. This cost is invisible in any tax return and often larger than the tax.

Put an illustrative figure on it. A hypothetical company worth 9,000,000 dollars with a named, trained successor might sell to an informed buyer near that value. The same company, offered by heirs who are visibly in dispute and have no manager, might attract offers several hundred thousand dollars to well over a million dollars lower, because the buyer is pricing in the risk of taking over a business with no leader and the knowledge that the sellers need to sell. The exact discount cannot be predicted. The direction can. Every year of preparation you invest in a successor narrows that discount, and that is a return you can actually earn.

The third cost is the equalisation gap: the cash needed to give inactive heirs fair value when the active heir keeps the business. I will define it carefully, because it is this week's working term. If the family decides that the active heir keeps the operating company and the others receive equal value, the equalisation gap is the value the others are owed minus what the rest of the estate can provide.

A worked example

A hypothetical estate after debts: an operating development company worth 9,000,000 dollars, a rental building worth 4,500,000 dollars, and cash and investments of 1,500,000 dollars. Total: 15,000,000 dollars. Three children. The family agrees each should receive equal value, and that the eldest, who runs the company, keeps all of it.

Step 1. Equal share: 15,000,000 divided by 3 is 5,000,000 dollars each.

Step 2. The eldest receives the company at 9,000,000 dollars, which is 4,000,000 dollars more than an equal share.

Step 3. The other two need 5,000,000 dollars each, 10,000,000 dollars in total. The rest of the estate, the building plus cash, is 6,000,000 dollars.

Step 4. Equalisation gap: 10,000,000 minus 6,000,000 is 4,000,000 dollars. That is exactly the eldest's excess, as it must be.

Step 5. Add an assumed transfer cost. Suppose, purely for illustration, that taxes and fees at death take 1,500,000 dollars, payable in cash. Now the estate has only 4,500,000 dollars of non-company assets and owes the two siblings 10,000,000 dollars of value. The real gap is 5,500,000 dollars, and it is cash.

Say that out loud now.

Four ways to close the gap

First, life insurance owned in a way that keeps the proceeds available to the estate or the heirs, sized to the gap plus the transfer cost. It converts a future cash shortage into a known annual premium. Warrick's caution: the right ownership structure and the tax treatment of the proceeds depend on local law, and a licensed adviser is required before you act.

Second, an equalisation note: the active heir owes the siblings the gap and pays it over years from the company's earnings. In the example, 4,000,000 dollars over ten years at an assumed interest rate. It keeps the business intact, but it makes the siblings creditors of their brother for a decade, which needs security and a clear default rule.

Third, reallocating other assets: give the siblings more of the passive assets now, through gifts or an estate freeze that sends future growth to them, so the gap is smaller at death.

Fourth, accepting unequal value, openly. The family may decide that the eldest's years of work justify part of his excess. If so, the founder writes down the reasoning, explains it to all three, and ideally has the siblings acknowledge it in writing. An unexplained unequal will is an invitation to a court challenge; an explained one is a family decision.

Applied comparison, same estate. Insurance of 5,500,000 dollars costs an annual premium the founder pays while alive. The note costs the eldest 4,000,000 dollars plus interest over ten years, which reduces the cash the company can reinvest and may weaken its borrowing capacity. Reallocation costs nothing in cash but requires the founder to give away control of some assets earlier than she might like. There is no free option. The choice is about who bears the cost and when.

Wealth Ledger

For your own personal balance sheet, Mr Shabazz, add one line beneath net worth: succession liquidity need, the cash your estate would need on a bad day to pay transfer costs and keep any promises of fairness. Set it against your liquid assets. If the need exceeds the liquidity, you have a hidden concentration risk that only shows up at death. The fix is not to stop building illiquid wealth; it is to fund the gap deliberately, with insurance, reallocation or a written note, and to revisit it every time a project raises your net worth.

Professional sign-off required: tax adviser and estate lawyer, on transfer cost and structure; licensed insurance adviser, on any policy.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is an estate rich in value and poor in cash, where the transfer costs and fairness promises can only be met by selling the asset the family most wanted to keep. The control is a written succession liquidity figure, recalculated each year, with a named funding source for every dollar of it.

The beginner's mistake

Calculating equal shares on paper and stopping there. The beginner never asks whether the estate holds the cash to make the shares equal in practice, so the arithmetic is right and the outcome is a forced sale.

Callback

In Week 88, Warrick and Priya treated insurance as architecture rather than a product: a tool for moving a specific risk off the balance sheet. The equalisation gap is one such risk, with a known size and a known trigger, which makes it one of the clearest uses of life insurance in a developer's plan.

Recap

Succession costs transfer tax and fees, value lost in a bad handover, and the equalisation gap. Close the gap with insurance, a note, early reallocation or an openly explained unequal division, and track a succession liquidity figure on your own balance sheet.

Next: Tessa, on The Rules: what makes a family constitution binding, and where the law limits what a founder can decide.
checklist: I know my estate's three succession costs, at least as ranges.
I have calculated the equalisation gap for my intended division.
Every dollar of that gap has a named funding source.
Any equalisation note has security and a default rule.
Any unequal division is written down with its reasons and explained.
My balance sheet shows a succession liquidity line.
I recalculate the gap whenever my net worth moves materially.
head: Field checklist
speak: Succession costs money in three ways. Transfer cost is tax and fees when ownership moves, and it depends entirely on the jurisdiction. Value leakage is what the business loses when it changes hands without a ready leader. The equalisation gap is the cash needed to give inactive heirs fair value when the active heir keeps the business. In a hypothetical 15,000,000 dollar estate where the company is worth 9,000,000, an equal share is 5,000,000 each, the eldest is 4,000,000 over, and after an assumed 1,500,000 of transfer costs the real gap is 5,500,000 dollars of cash the estate does not have. Close it with insurance, an equalisation note paid over years, early reallocation of passive assets, or an openly explained unequal division. Put a succession liquidity line on your own balance sheet, give every dollar of it a funding source, and recalculate it each year.
terms: Equalisation gap — the value owed to inactive heirs, in a plan where the active heir keeps the business, minus what the rest of the estate can provide.
Value leakage — the loss in a business's value when ownership or leadership changes badly, from lost staff, tighter credit or a forced sale.
Equalisation note — a debt the active heir owes the inactive heirs, paid over time, used to balance an unequal division of assets.

hostile.q: Your estate plan promises your two inactive children equal value. Where is the cash, and does your company's debt capacity survive paying it?
hostile.a: The gap is covered by insurance sized to it plus an estimate of transfer costs, so the company pays nothing at my death. If that fails, the fallback note is capped at an amount that keeps the company inside its covenants on our current base case, and I will show you that test.

title: What Makes a Family Constitution Bind, and Where the Law Steps In
summary: A family constitution states intentions; the shareholders' agreement, articles, trust deed and will give them legal force. The law also limits a founder's freedom: claims by dependants, challenges for lack of capacity or undue influence, and the rights of a spouse. This lesson maps those rules and compares, in concept, how Canada and Guyana approach them.
body:
A family constitution is a promise, not a contract, until the documents beneath it carry its terms. And even a perfectly drafted plan sits inside rules that let certain people challenge it, so build it to survive a challenge.

Recall

Q. What two dangers arise when someone signs more than one will for different countries?

A. That a later will revokes an earlier one by its general wording, and that gaps or overlaps leave an asset covered by no will or by two. Each will must state the assets it covers and preserve the other.

Q. What is a deemed disposition, in concept?

A. A rule in some tax systems that treats a person as having sold property at fair market value on an event, such as death or leaving the country, even though no sale happened. Verify whether and how it applies against the primary source.

Q. What is an ownership layer in wealth architecture?

A. One level in the chain of holding entities between you and an asset, such as a holding company owning a project company. Each layer is chosen for a purpose: liability, tax, control or estate.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, families spend months agreeing a constitution, then discover it cannot stop a sibling from selling shares to an outsider, because nothing in the share documents says so. Others write a will that disinherits a child or a spouse and are surprised when a court varies it. The rules in this lesson decide whether a succession plan does what it says. I teach the concepts. The answer in any real case depends on the jurisdiction, the documents and the facts, and needs a lawyer.

Moral force and legal force

Plain English. A family constitution is usually written in the language of intention: "we believe", "we will aim to", "family members should". Courts generally enforce obligations that parties intended to be legally binding and stated clearly. A statement of values is rarely that. So most constitutions say, in terms, that they are not legally binding, and many lawyers recommend exactly that, because a binding constitution invites family litigation over every clause.

The professional framing is a two-tier structure. The constitution is the first tier: values and principles. The second tier is the set of implementing documents, the legal instruments that turn chosen principles into enforceable rules: the shareholders' agreement, the company's articles or by-laws, the trust deed, any partnership agreement, and the will. A principle not carried into the second tier is a hope.

Applied example. A hypothetical constitution says family shares should stay in the family. The second tier carries that out through a right of first refusal in the shareholders' agreement, so a family member wishing to sell must first offer to the others at a formula price, and a restriction in the articles so the company will not register a transfer that skips that step. Now an outside sale is not merely frowned upon; it does not complete.

Limits on freedom to divide

Common law systems traditionally gave a person wide testamentary freedom, the freedom to leave property to whoever they choose. That freedom is now limited in several ways, which differ by jurisdiction.

First, claims by dependants. Many jurisdictions let a spouse, a child or another dependant ask a court to vary a will that leaves them without adequate support. The test, who may claim, and the time limit for claiming all vary. Verify against the primary source before you rely on it.

Second, family property rights. In some places a surviving spouse has rights in family property that operate alongside or above the will, so a will cannot simply leave a spouse out.

Third, validity challenges. A will or a gift can be attacked for lack of capacity, meaning the person did not understand what they were doing, or for undue influence, meaning someone overpowered their free choice. A founder who leaves more to the child who cared for them in old age is a classic target.

Say that out loud now.

Applied example. A hypothetical founder, aged 80, signs a new will two months before death, leaving the company to the one child who lives with him and nothing to the others. The others challenge it. The plan's defences are documentary: a lawyer who met the founder alone, notes of the founder's own reasons, a capacity assessment if there was any doubt, and ideally an earlier history showing the same intention. Fairness explained and recorded over years is far harder to overturn than a late surprise.

Two Systems

A conceptual comparison only. Verify against primary source before relying on any point.

Canada. Succession law is mostly provincial, so the rules differ across the country. Most provinces follow the common law tradition; Quebec follows a civil law tradition with its own code, and its rules on succession and family property differ from the other provinces. Several provinces have legislation allowing dependants to claim support from an estate, and family property regimes can give spouses rights that interact with the will. The details, including who counts as a dependant and the deadlines, are province specific.

Guyana. Guyana's legal system is in the common law tradition, having moved from its earlier Roman-Dutch roots to English common law in the early twentieth century [unverified — confirm independently]. Wills, probate and the administration of estates follow that tradition, under Guyanese statute and court practice. Whether and how dependants or spouses may claim against a will, and the limits on doing so, must be confirmed with a Guyanese lawyer [unverified — confirm independently].

The practical point for a family with assets in both: the two systems may treat the same family differently, so the constitution's principles must be implemented separately, in documents valid in each place.

The duties that follow control

When an heir takes control, they take on legal duties. A director owes duties to the company, not to their siblings. A trustee owes duties to all beneficiaries, including the ones they dislike. A family constitution that says "the eldest decides for the family" cannot override those duties. Teach the successor what they will owe before they take the seat.

Applied example. A hypothetical eldest daughter becomes sole trustee of a family trust that holds a rental building, and her two brothers are beneficiaries. She also runs the family's construction company, which bids to renovate the building. She may believe the price is fair. The law sees a trustee contracting with herself, a conflict that typically requires disclosure, independent pricing and, depending on the trust deed and local law, the consent of the beneficiaries or a court. A constitution that says "family members get first call on family work" does not displace that duty. The fix is a written conflicts procedure in the trust deed and a second, independent trustee who decides any matter in which the first is interested.

Professional sign-off required: estate lawyer in each relevant jurisdiction; corporate lawyer, on share restrictions and the shareholders' agreement.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a plan that exists only in the constitution, or a will built to exclude someone the law protects, so the family discovers at death that its intentions are unenforceable or reversible. The control is a mapping table: every principle in the constitution beside the clause and document that enforces it, and every excluded or reduced heir beside the lawyer's advice on their possible claim.

The beginner's mistake

Making the constitution itself legally binding in the belief that this makes it stronger. It usually makes the family more litigious and the document more rigid. Keep the values tier flexible and put the enforceable rules in the documents designed to carry them.

Callback

In Week 20, LEX taught what binds in a letter of intent: clear terms intended to bind, separated from statements of intention that do not. A family constitution is the same split at family scale. The non-binding constitution is the letter of intent; the shareholders' agreement and trust deed are the contract.

Recap

A constitution states principles; implementing documents enforce them. Testamentary freedom is limited by dependants' claims, spousal property rights and challenges for capacity or undue influence. Canada's rules vary by province and by legal tradition; Guyana's follow the common law tradition and need local confirmation.

Next: Tessa, on The Numbers: a worked equalisation between an active heir and two inactive ones.
checklist: Every principle in my constitution maps to a clause in an enforceable document.
My constitution says clearly whether it is binding.
My share transfer restrictions sit in both the agreement and the articles.
I have advice on any claim an excluded or reduced heir could bring.
My reasons for any unequal division are recorded over time.
Each jurisdiction holding family assets has documents valid there.
Any successor knows the legal duties of a director and trustee.
head: Field checklist
speak: A family constitution usually states values and intentions, and most are written to be non-binding on purpose, because a binding one invites litigation over every clause. Its rules gain legal force only through implementing documents: the shareholders' agreement, the articles, the trust deed and the will. A principle not carried into those documents is a hope. The law also limits a founder's freedom to divide: dependants may claim against a will that leaves them without support, spouses may have family property rights, and a will can be challenged for lack of capacity or undue influence. The defence is documentary: independent advice, recorded reasons, and the same intention shown over years. In Canada these rules are largely provincial, with Quebec in the civil law tradition. Guyana follows the common law tradition and must be confirmed locally. Implement the plan separately in each place, and teach any successor the duties that come with control.
terms: Implementing documents — the legal instruments, such as a shareholders' agreement, articles, trust deed and will, that turn family principles into enforceable rules.
Testamentary freedom — the freedom to leave property by will to whomever you choose, limited by rules protecting dependants and spouses.
Undue influence — pressure that overpowers a person's free will in making a will or gift, a ground for setting it aside.

hostile.q: Your constitution says the shares stay in the family. Show me what actually stops your sister selling hers to a competitor.
hostile.a: The shareholders' agreement gives the other shareholders a right of first refusal at a formula price, and the articles bar the company from registering any transfer that has not gone through that procedure. I will send you both clauses; the constitution itself is deliberately non-binding.

title: Working an Equalisation: Sweat Equity, the Note and the Insurance
summary: A step-by-step equalisation for a hypothetical family: separate the value the active heir created from the value she inherited, set the fair shares, size the gap, then test whether a note or insurance closes it. Every number is a round hypothetical.
body:
Fairness becomes a number once you separate the value an heir created from the value they inherit. Do that arithmetic in writing, and the family argues about one figure rather than about everything.

Recall

Q. What makes a family constitution's rules enforceable?

A. Carrying each principle into an implementing document, such as the shareholders' agreement, articles, trust deed or will. The constitution itself is usually non-binding by design.

Q. In a deemed disposition at death, what value is the property usually treated as sold at?

A. Fair market value at the time of the event, in systems that use the concept. That is why a valuation matters to the tax bill. Verify the rule against the primary source.

Q. Why do currency reserves matter to a family with assets in two countries?

A. Because obligations, such as tax, fees or a payout to an heir, may fall due in one currency while the assets are in another. Holding a reserve in the currency of the obligation avoids a forced sale at a bad exchange rate.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, families rarely fight over arithmetic they have seen. They fight over arithmetic that was never shown. If the active heir believes she earned half the company's value and her brothers believe she merely inherited it, no plan survives. This lesson makes the disagreement visible and measurable. All figures are hypothetical, and the tax line is an illustrative assumption, not a rate.

Step 1: value the estate

A hypothetical estate after debts:

AssetValue in dollars
Operating development company10,000,000
Rental building3,000,000
Cash and investments2,000,000
Total15,000,000

Three children. The daughter has run the company for twelve years. The two sons have not worked in it.

Step 2: separate created value from inherited value

This is the step most families skip. When the daughter joined, an independent valuation put the company at 4,000,000 dollars. It is now worth 10,000,000 dollars. So 6,000,000 dollars of growth happened on her watch. Not all of that is hers: some came from rising land values, some from capital the founder contributed, and some from the founder's own work. The family must agree a share.

Suppose, after discussion, the family agrees that one third of the growth reflects the daughter's work beyond what her salary paid for. That is sweat equity: value attributed to a person's unpaid or underpaid effort, as distinct from capital or inheritance. One third of 6,000,000 is 2,000,000 dollars.

The figure is a judgement, not a calculation. The point is that it is now one agreed number, written down, rather than a feeling that varies by sibling and by evening.

Say that out loud now.

Step 3: set the fair shares

Take the sweat equity off the top. 15,000,000 minus 2,000,000 is 13,000,000 dollars to divide equally. 13,000,000 divided by 3 is 4,333,333 dollars each, call it 4,330,000 for speaking.

Fair shares: daughter 2,000,000 plus 4,330,000, which is 6,330,000 dollars. Each son 4,330,000 dollars. Total 14,990,000, the difference being rounding.

Notice what fairness did. Equality would give each child 5,000,000 dollars. The agreed fair division gives the daughter 1,330,000 dollars more than equal and each son about 670,000 dollars less. That is the conversation the founder must lead while alive.

Step 4: size the gap

The family wants the daughter to keep the whole company. She receives 10,000,000 dollars of company against a fair share of 6,330,000 dollars, so she is over by 3,670,000 dollars.

The sons are owed 4,330,000 each, 8,660,000 dollars in total. The non-company assets are 5,000,000 dollars. Gap before costs: 3,660,000 dollars, matching the daughter's excess, allowing for rounding.

Now add an illustrative transfer cost of 1,000,000 dollars payable in cash at death. Non-company assets left: 4,000,000 dollars. Gap after costs: 8,660,000 minus 4,000,000, which is 4,660,000 dollars.

Step 5: test a note

Option one: the daughter owes her brothers 4,660,000 dollars through an equalisation note, paid over 10 years. Ignoring interest, that is 466,000 dollars a year. Add interest at an assumed 6 percent on the declining balance and the first year's payment is roughly 466,000 plus 280,000, which is about 746,000 dollars.

Test it against the company. Suppose the company generates 1,200,000 dollars a year of free cash after debt service. Paying 746,000 leaves 454,000 dollars for reinvestment, a reserve and her own pay. That is thin for a developer who needs equity for new sites. And the cash leaving the company may first need to be paid to her personally, possibly creating tax on the way out. The note works on paper and starves the business in practice.

Step 6: test insurance and a blend

Option two: life insurance on the founder sized at 4,660,000 dollars, held so the proceeds reach the estate or the sons, depending on local law and advice. The annual cost is a premium the founder pays during life. At death the sons receive cash and the company pays nothing.

Option three, often the best: a blend. Insure 3,000,000 dollars, leave a note of 1,660,000 dollars over 10 years, which is about 166,000 dollars a year before interest, well inside the company's cash flow. The sons receive most of their value at once and the rest on a schedule the business can carry.

A second example: the valuation moves

Valuations are estimates, so test the plan against a different one. Suppose a second valuer puts the company at 8,000,000 dollars instead of 10,000,000. The estate is now 13,000,000 dollars. Growth on the daughter's watch is 4,000,000, and one third of it is about 1,330,000 dollars of sweat equity. 13,000,000 minus 1,330,000 is 11,670,000 dollars, or 3,890,000 each. The daughter's fair share is 5,220,000; each son's 3,890,000.

She keeps a company now worth 8,000,000 dollars, so she is over by 2,780,000. The sons are owed 7,780,000 in total against 4,000,000 of non-company assets after the same 1,000,000 of costs, a gap of 3,780,000 dollars. The 3,000,000 of insurance now covers most of it, and the note falls to 780,000 dollars. Two lessons follow. The gap moves with the valuation, so the insurance should be reviewed when the company's value moves. And the sweat equity rule should be written as a share of growth, not a fixed dollar figure, so it scales with the valuation instead of needing to be renegotiated.

Step 7: write the result down

The output is one page: the valuation, the agreed sweat equity and its reasoning, the fair shares, the gap, and the funding. All three children read it while the founder is alive. That page is the best defence against a later claim of unfairness, because it shows the reasoning was explained, not imposed at death.

Professional sign-off required: independent business valuer; estate lawyer; tax adviser; licensed insurance adviser.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a note sized to the arithmetic rather than to the company's cash flow, so fairness to the inactive heirs bankrupts the business the active heir kept. The control is to test every note against the company's free cash after debt service, with a downside case, before agreeing it.

The beginner's mistake

Using today's company value as if the active heir created none of it, or as if she created all of it. Both extremes are easy and both are wrong. Agree a starting valuation and a sweat equity share, in writing.

Callback

In Week 44, Roman taught stress tests: run the base, downside and severe cases before you rely on a number. An equalisation note is a debt service obligation like any other, and it deserves the same test. A note that only works in the base case is a note that fails in the year the family can least afford a fight.

Recap

Value the estate, separate sweat equity from inheritance, set fair shares, size the gap after transfer costs, and test any note against the company's cash flow. A blend of insurance and a modest note often works best. Put it on one page the whole family reads.

Next: Kema, on The Room: the family meeting where the active heir asks for control.
checklist: I start from an independent valuation, not an opinion.
I record the company's value when the active heir joined.
The family has agreed a written sweat equity figure and its reasons.
I calculate fair shares after deducting sweat equity.
I size the gap after an estimate of transfer costs.
I test any note against the company's free cash in a downside case.
Every child has read the one-page result while I am alive.
head: Field checklist
speak: Here is a hypothetical equalisation. The estate is 15,000,000 dollars: a company at 10,000,000, a building at 3,000,000 and 2,000,000 in cash. The daughter has run the company for twelve years; it grew from 4,000,000 to 10,000,000 on her watch. The family agrees one third of that growth, 2,000,000 dollars, is her sweat equity. The remaining 13,000,000 split three ways gives about 4,330,000 each, so the daughter's fair share is 6,330,000 and each son's 4,330,000. She keeps the company and is 3,670,000 over. After an assumed 1,000,000 of transfer costs, the sons are short 4,660,000 dollars. A ten-year note would cost the company about 746,000 dollars in its first year, which starves a developer. A blend works better: insurance for 3,000,000 and a note for 1,660,000. Put the whole calculation on one page every child reads while the founder is alive.
terms: Sweat equity — value attributed to a person's underpaid or unpaid work in a business, as distinct from capital contributed or inherited.
Fair share — the value a family agrees each heir should receive, which may differ from an equal share.
Free cash after debt service — the cash a business generates after operating costs and loan payments, the pool from which any equalisation note must be paid.

hostile.q: Your sons will say your daughter's sweat equity figure is invented. Why should they accept 2,000,000 dollars?
hostile.a: Because it was agreed in writing by all three of them, during my life, against an independent valuation at the date she joined and today's valuation. The share of growth attributed to her is a judgement, and the record shows it was discussed and accepted, not imposed.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: The Family Meeting Where an Heir Asks for Control
summary: A realistic scene: a hypothetical founder's family meeting at which the active heir asks for control of the company and a sibling asks why equal is not fair. The lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind each question, when to stay silent and how to hold your state.
body:
A family meeting about succession is a negotiation among people who will still be family afterwards. Your job as the founder is not to win it; it is to make the reasoning visible and leave every person able to agree without losing face.

Recall

Q. In the equalisation example, why did a ten-year note on its own fail?

A. Because its first-year payment consumed most of the company's free cash after debt service, leaving too little for reinvestment. A blend of insurance and a smaller note fitted the business.

Q. What is the difference between a fixed and a discretionary trust?

A. In a fixed trust each beneficiary's share is set by the deed. In a discretionary trust the trustee decides who receives income or capital, within the deed's powers and the trustee's duties.

Q. What does position sizing mean in personal capital allocation?

A. Deciding how much of your wealth goes into any single investment, so that one loss, however bad, cannot destroy the whole.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, every document this week needs a conversation first. The founder who avoids that conversation leaves the family to have it at the reading of the will, the worst possible moment. This scene is hypothetical. You play the founder, a developer in his sixties. Present are your daughter, who runs the company; your son, a teacher; and an independent facilitator, a family business adviser you have hired so you are not also chairing.

The scene

You open, as agreed, with the bottom line: "I want to settle three things today. Who runs the company after me, how the value is shared, and how we decide when we disagree. Nothing will be signed today. Everything will be written down."

Your daughter speaks first. "I've run this company for twelve years. I want the voting shares, and I want them while you're here to back me, not after."

Your son: "I don't want to run anything. But I don't understand why equal isn't fair. We're both your children."

The question behind the question

Your daughter is not really asking for shares. She is asking whether her twelve years are seen. Her request for control now rather than later is a request for protection: she has watched what happens when authority arrives with grief and no backing.

Your son is not really asking for money. He is asking whether he matters as much as the child who works with you every day. If you answer his question with numbers, he will hear that he does not.

Say that out loud now.

Lines to say

To your daughter: "You've built most of what this company is now. I want the plan to say that in writing. I'm open to moving voting control to you in stages, starting this year, with an independent director on the board so you're never alone in a dispute."

To your son: "You matter exactly as much. Equal love doesn't mean the same asset. I don't want to hand you a business you'd have to run or fight over. I want you to receive the same fairness in a form that's yours outright."

To both: "Here is one page that shows how I've thought about the value. I want you to challenge it. If it's wrong, I'd rather know now."

And then: "What would make this feel fair to you?" Ask it of each, separately, and write the answers down.

Lines never to say

"You'll get what I decide." It ends the conversation and starts the court case.

"Your sister earned it and you didn't." It turns a question of role into a question of worth.

"Let's not talk about money, we're family." The money is exactly what will divide them if it is not talked about.

"This is all decided already." Even if your mind is largely made up, a plan presented as final invites resistance rather than ownership. Present it as a draft and mean it.

When to stay silent

After your son says "we're both your children", stay silent for several seconds. He has said the hardest thing in the room. Filling the silence with an explanation tells him you were waiting to rebut him. Let the facilitator acknowledge it, or simply nod, then answer.

After you ask "what would make this feel fair?", stay silent until they answer, however long it takes. The first person to fill that silence usually reveals the real issue.

And when your two children start to argue with each other, do not rescue either. Let the facilitator manage it. A founder who intervenes picks a side, whatever he intends.

Holding your state

You will feel defensive: this is a meeting about your death and your judgement. Before the meeting, decide your one non-negotiable and your three things you are open on, and write them on a card you can glance at. During it, slow your speaking pace and lower your volume when you feel your chest tighten; a calm voice is the single most persuasive thing in that room. Do the arithmetic before the meeting, not in it. If you feel anger rising, say "Let me think about that and come back to you this week", and mean it.

The second hard moment

Midway through, your daughter adds: "And I want a market salary from now on. I've been underpaid for years." Your son looks at you. This is where many meetings break, because the request sounds like money taken from him.

Say: "That's reasonable, and it actually makes the rest simpler. If you're paid a market rate from now on, the company's future growth is no longer partly your unpaid work, so the sweat equity question stops growing every year." Then turn to your son: "It also means the value you inherit isn't quietly shrinking because your sister is subsidising the business with her pay." You have converted a grievance into a rule that protects both of them.

Never say: "We'll sort out pay later." Later is how a founder dies with an underpaid successor and an unrecorded grievance, which is exactly the composite case from Day 2.

How it ends

A good outcome is not agreement. It is three written lists: what everyone agrees, what is still open, and who will do what before the next meeting. Your daughter leaves knowing control is coming and when. Your son leaves having been asked what fairness means to him. The facilitator circulates notes within a week.

Family, legacy and what "enough" means

This month's thread, Mr Shabazz, is a question for you rather than an answer. Before you hold any meeting like this one, you will need to know what you are actually trying to leave behind: a company, an amount of money, a set of skills in your children, a reputation, or something else. Families who skip that question tend to divide assets efficiently and pass on very little.

So the question for your own notebook: how much would be enough for the people you are responsible for, and what would you want them to have that money cannot buy? I will not suggest an answer. Write yours down, date it, and see whether it changes when you read it again in a year.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is the founder treating the meeting as an announcement, so the family nods in the room and fights afterwards. The control is an independent facilitator, a draft rather than a decision, and written notes that record what each person said fairness means.

The beginner's mistake

Holding one big meeting and expecting it to settle everything. Succession is a series of conversations over months or years. The first meeting's job is to start it well.

Callback

In Week 66, Kema and JAX separated positions from interests. Your daughter's position is "voting shares now"; her interest is recognition and protection. Your son's position is "equal shares"; his interest is to know he matters. A succession plan that serves the interests can usually accommodate the positions, and one that only trades positions leaves the interests unmet.

Recap

Open with the bottom line, hear the question behind each question, say what recognises both children, never compare their worth, stay silent after the hard sentences, and end with written lists. The meeting starts the plan; it does not finish it.

Next: Kema, on Quiz and Recap: six questions on succession and a Red Pen on a draft family constitution.
checklist: I hire an independent facilitator so I am not also chairing.
I open with the three things I want to settle and that nothing is signed today.
I identify the interest behind each family member's position.
I ask each person what would make the plan feel fair, and write it down.
I never compare my children's worth.
I stay silent after the hardest sentence in the room.
The meeting ends with three written lists and a date for the next one.
head: Field checklist
speak: A family succession meeting is a negotiation among people who stay family afterwards. Bring an independent facilitator so you are not also chairing. Open with the bottom line: today we settle who runs the company, how value is shared, and how we decide when we disagree; nothing is signed, everything is written. Listen for the question behind each question. The active heir asking for control now is asking whether her work is seen and whether she will be protected. The sibling asking why equal is not fair is asking whether he matters. Recognise the first with staged control and an independent director, and answer the second with care before numbers: equal love does not mean the same asset. Never compare their worth, never say it is already decided. Stay silent after the hardest sentence. End with three lists: agreed, still open, and who does what before the next meeting.
terms: Independent facilitator — a neutral adviser who chairs a family meeting so the founder can participate without also controlling the process.
Staged transfer of control — moving voting control to a successor in steps over time, often with safeguards at each step.
Family assembly — a regular meeting of the wider family, separate from the board, for family matters rather than business decisions.

hostile.q: Your son asks, in front of everyone: if you trusted me as much as her, why does she get the company?
hostile.a: Because she has chosen to run it and you have chosen a different life, and I respect both choices. Trust is not the issue; roles are. You will receive the same fair value in a form you own outright, and I want you to tell me what would make that feel fair.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 93 Review: Succession, Fairness and the Family Constitution
summary: Six questions on succession with answers, a recap of the week, a Red Pen drill on a draft family constitution clause, and a two-minute boardroom drill explaining how a founder passes on a company without breaking the family.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: a succession plan moves ownership, control and knowledge separately, explains fairness while the founder is alive, and puts every family rule into a document that can enforce it.

Recall

Q. In the family meeting, what is the question behind an active heir's request for voting control now?

A. Whether her years of work are seen, and whether she will be protected when authority arrives, rather than inheriting it in grief with no backing.

Q. What does a right of first refusal do in a shareholders' agreement?

A. It requires a shareholder who wants to sell to offer the shares first to the other shareholders, usually at a formula price or the outsider's price, before selling outside.

Q. Why does correlation matter when you invest beyond real estate?

A. Because assets that fall together in the same conditions do not protect each other. Diversification only works across assets whose values do not move in lockstep.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, if you can answer these six questions aloud without notes, you can sit with an estate lawyer and a family business adviser and steer the conversation instead of following it. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. What are the three handovers in succession, and which one can a will move?

Answer: Ownership, control and knowledge. A will moves ownership. Control needs share structure, board seats and signing authority. Knowledge moves only through years of supervised work.

Question 2. What is a family constitution, and where does its legal force come from?

Answer: A written agreement among family members on values, governance and decision rules for shared assets. It is usually non-binding by design. Its force comes from implementing documents: the shareholders' agreement, articles, trust deed and will.

Question 3. What is the difference between fairness and equality among heirs?

Answer: Equality gives everyone the same. Fairness gives each person what the family agrees is right given contribution, need and role. Equal shares can be unfair, and unequal ones can be fair if explained and accepted.

Question 4. What is the equalisation gap, and name three ways to close it.

Answer: The value owed to inactive heirs, when the active heir keeps the business, minus what the rest of the estate can provide after transfer costs. Close it with life insurance, an equalisation note, early reallocation of passive assets, or an openly explained unequal division.

Question 5. Why is an equalisation note dangerous if sized only to the arithmetic?

Answer: Because the company must pay it from free cash after debt service. A note sized to the gap can starve the business of reinvestment, weaken its borrowing capacity, and fail in a downside year.

Question 6. What makes an unequal will harder to challenge?

Answer: Independent legal advice, a record of the founder's own reasons, any capacity evidence needed, and the same intention shown consistently over years. A late surprise is the easiest kind to attack.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Tessa separated succession into ownership, control and knowledge, and placed the family constitution above the documents that enforce it. Ford and Cole took a composite case in which equal votes to three heirs ended in a discounted sale, giving Rule 93. Warrick priced transfer cost, value leakage and the equalisation gap. Tessa mapped what makes a constitution bind and where dependants and validity challenges limit a founder's freedom, with a Canada and Guyana comparison. Tessa then worked an equalisation with sweat equity and a blended note and insurance. Kema ran the family meeting.

The Red Pen

Here is a hypothetical draft clause from a family constitution. Find the defects before reading on.

Clause 7. Family Business. (a) All children shall inherit the Company equally and shall each be directors. (b) The Company shall be run by whichever child is most experienced at the time. (c) Family members employed by the Company shall be paid what the family considers appropriate. (d) This constitution is legally binding on all family members and overrides any other document. (e) Disputes shall be resolved amicably. (f) No family member may sell shares outside the family.

The defects. First, clause (a) hands out equal value, equal votes and a board seat together, the exact pattern behind Day 2's failure, and makes directorship automatic rather than earned. Second, clause (b) names no person and no process: "most experienced" invites an argument about who that is, at the worst moment. Third, clause (c) sets pay by family feeling rather than a written market rate, which is how an active heir ends up underpaid and resentful, and how sweat equity grows without anyone recording it. Fourth, clause (d) claims to be binding and to override other documents, which risks family litigation and may simply be ineffective against a shareholders' agreement, articles or a will; the enforceable rules belong in those documents. Fifth, clause (e) is a hope, not a mechanism: there is no deadlock rule, no independent director, no mediation step. Sixth, clause (f) prohibits an outside sale without saying who may buy, at what price, and what happens if no family member can afford it, so a sibling who needs cash is trapped.

The corrected version would name the successor or a selection process, separate voting from non-voting shares, set market pay, state that the constitution is non-binding and refer to the shareholders' agreement for enforceable terms, add a dispute ladder ending in an independent decision, and replace the outright ban with a right of first refusal at a formula price.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a partner who asks, "If you died next year, what happens to our company?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "Three things would need to move, not one. Ownership moves under my will and trust documents. Control is already settled: voting shares pass to my named successor, with an independent director on the board so no family disagreement can freeze a decision. Knowledge is the slow part, which is why my successor already attends our lender and contractor meetings. My family has a constitution that sets the principles, and the shareholders' agreement enforces them: a deadlock rule, a buy-sell clause with a formula price, and market pay for any family member employed. My other heirs receive fair value through insurance and passive assets, so the company does not have to pay them out. You would not be partnered with three people who cannot agree."

Score yourself. Did you open with the three handovers in one sentence? Did you say how deadlock breaks? Did you explain how inactive heirs are paid without draining the company? Did you finish inside two minutes? If not, record it again tomorrow.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is mistaking the will for the plan, so ownership passes while control and knowledge are left to chance. The control is a written succession map, a signed shareholders' agreement in your lifetime, and an annual review.

The beginner's mistake

Postponing the family conversation because it is uncomfortable. The founder is the only person with the authority to broker the agreement, and that authority ends without notice.

Callback

In Week 8, Tessa and Warrick taught the base layer: a will, powers of attorney, insurance and reserves. Succession is that same base built up a storey: the will now sits beneath a share structure, a shareholders' agreement and a constitution, and the insurance has a specific job, closing the equalisation gap.

Recap

Separate the three handovers, explain fairness while you can, fund the equalisation gap, and put every family rule into a document that enforces it. Rule 93 keeps multiple heirs from inheriting a deadlock.

checklist: What are the three handovers in succession, and which one can a will move?
What is a family constitution, and where does its legal force come from?
What is the difference between fairness and equality among heirs?
What is the equalisation gap, and name three ways to close it.
Why is an equalisation note dangerous if sized only to the arithmetic?
What makes an unequal will harder to challenge?
head: The six questions
speak: This week's core: succession moves three things. Ownership moves by will and trust. Control moves through share structure, board seats and signing authority. Knowledge moves only through years of supervised work. A family constitution states the family's principles and is usually non-binding; the shareholders' agreement, articles and trust deed enforce them. Fairness is not equality: an active heir may keep the company while the others receive equal value in other forms. The equalisation gap is the cash needed to make that work after transfer costs, and it is closed by insurance, a note the company can actually carry, early reallocation or an explained unequal division. An unequal will survives challenge when advice was independent and the reasons were recorded over years. Rule 93: never pass a company to more than one heir without a signed agreement, made in your lifetime, that names who decides, how deadlock breaks and how an exit is priced.
terms: Succession map — a written table naming, for ownership, control and knowledge, who receives each, when and on what condition.
Dispute ladder — a staged route for resolving disagreements, such as discussion, then mediation, then an independent decision.
Right of first refusal — a right for existing owners to buy shares a co-owner wishes to sell before they can be sold to an outsider.

hostile.q: You keep talking about fairness. Why should a lender care how you split your estate among your children?
hostile.a: Because how I split it decides who controls the borrower after me. If control is clear, deadlock is broken by a named mechanism and the heirs are paid without draining the company, your loan sees no change in management or cash flow on my death. That is what I have documented.
